questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Three domains of life: what places an organism in a domain
questions.question: A newly isolated unicellular organism has no nuclear membrane. Its cell wall has no peptidoglycan, and the sequence of its small-subunit ribosomal RNA is closer to that of yeast than to that of Escherichia coli. In the three-domain system, where is it placed, and why?
options: A) Bacteria, because every cell without a nuclear membrane belongs to this domain
B) Archaea, because the domains are separated by ribosomal RNA sequence and cell chemistry, not only by the absence of a nucleus
C) Eukarya, because its ribosomal RNA is closer to that of a eukaryote than to that of a bacterium
D) Kingdom Monera of the domain Eukarya, because Monera contains all organisms without a nucleus
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Archaea, because the domains are separated by ribosomal RNA sequence and cell chemistry, not only by the absence of a nucleus.
Concept: The three-domain system divides life into Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya. Both Bacteria and Archaea are prokaryotic, so the absence of a nucleus cannot separate them. They are separated by ribosomal RNA sequence and by cell-wall and membrane chemistry.
Why: The organism is prokaryotic, so it is not in Eukarya. Its wall lacks peptidoglycan, which is the wall polymer of Bacteria, and its ribosomal RNA is nearer to a eukaryote than to a bacterium. Both observations are features of Archaea. The five-kingdom system would put it in Monera, but the three-domain system splits Monera into two domains.
Why not the others: (A) A missing nucleus is shared by Bacteria and Archaea; the wall without peptidoglycan rules out Bacteria. (C) Being closer to eukaryotes in one sequence does not make a cell eukaryotic; it still has no nucleus. (D) Monera is a kingdom of the five-kingdom system and is not a part of the domain Eukarya.
Key point: Prokaryote is a cell type, not a domain; Archaea and Bacteria are told apart by ribosomal RNA and wall chemistry.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Germ layers, symmetry and coelom as the basis of animal classification
questions.question:
The table gives four features of animals P, Q, R and S.

Animal | Symmetry | Germ layers | Body cavity between gut and body wall | Metameric segmentation
P | radial | two | absent | absent
Q | bilateral | three | absent | absent
R | bilateral | three | present; mesoderm occurs as scattered pouches | absent
S | bilateral | three | present | present

S has a true coelom. Which statement follows from the table?
options: A) Q and R both have a fluid-filled cavity between the gut and the body wall
B) P has three germ layers but no body cavity
C) In R the mesoderm forms a continuous lining around the body cavity
D) Only in S is the body cavity lined on all sides by mesoderm
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Only in S is the body cavity lined on all sides by mesoderm.
Concept: Animals are grouped by symmetry, number of germ layers and the nature of the body cavity. A true coelom is a cavity lined by mesoderm. In a pseudocoelom the mesoderm is present only as scattered pouches between ectoderm and endoderm. An acoelomate has no cavity.
Why: P is diploblastic and has no mesoderm at all. Q is triploblastic but acoelomate. R has a cavity that is not lined by mesoderm, so it is a pseudocoelomate. S is stated to have a true coelom, so only S has a cavity lined by mesoderm.
Why not the others: (A) Q has no body cavity; only R and S have one. (B) P has two germ layers, not three. (C) Scattered pouches of mesoderm are the mark of a pseudocoelom, not of a continuous lining.
Key point: Coelom lined by mesoderm = coelomate; cavity not lined by mesoderm = pseudocoelomate; no cavity = acoelomate.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Epidermal tissue system: stomata and cuticle
questions.question: A mutant plant forms leaves that have no guard cells. The other epidermal cells and the waxy cuticle are normal, and the vascular bundles are normal. The plant is kept well watered in bright light. What is the most direct effect on its leaves?
options: A) Entry of carbon dioxide into the leaf falls sharply, because very little gas passes through a cuticle-covered epidermis
B) Water loss becomes uncontrolled, because the stomatal pores stay open all the time
C) Water cannot reach the mesophyll, because xylem vessels are part of the epidermal tissue system
D) There is no effect, because gas exchange in leaves takes place mainly through the vascular bundles
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Entry of carbon dioxide into the leaf falls sharply, because very little gas passes through a cuticle-covered epidermis.
Concept: The epidermal tissue system consists of epidermal cells, stomata and epidermal appendages. Each stoma is a pore enclosed by two guard cells. The cuticle on the epidermis prevents loss of water and is almost impermeable to gases.
Why: Without guard cells no stomatal pore is formed. The only remaining path for gases is through the cuticle, which lets very little through. So carbon dioxide entry, and with it photosynthesis, falls sharply even though light and water are available.
Why not the others: (B) A pore cannot stay open if it was never formed; without guard cells there are no stomata. (C) Xylem belongs to the vascular tissue system, which is stated to be normal. (D) Vascular bundles conduct water and food; they do not exchange gases with the air.
Key point: Stomata are part of the epidermal tissue system and are the main route of gas exchange in a leaf.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Eukaryotic and prokaryotic cells: route of a secreted protein
questions.question: A pancreatic cell and a bacterium each make an enzyme that is released outside the cell. Which sequence is in the correct order and is possible only in the pancreatic cell?
options: A) Ribosome free in the cytoplasm → cytoplasm → plasma membrane → outside
B) Ribosome on rough endoplasmic reticulum → Golgi cisternae → lumen of endoplasmic reticulum → secretory vesicle → outside
C) Ribosome on rough endoplasmic reticulum → lumen of endoplasmic reticulum → Golgi cisternae → secretory vesicle → plasma membrane → outside
D) Ribosome on rough endoplasmic reticulum → lysosome → Golgi cisternae → plasma membrane → outside
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Ribosome on rough endoplasmic reticulum → lumen of endoplasmic reticulum → Golgi cisternae → secretory vesicle → plasma membrane → outside.
Concept: Eukaryotic cells have an endomembrane system: endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles. Prokaryotic cells have ribosomes but no membrane-bound organelles.
Why: A secreted protein of a eukaryotic cell is made on ribosomes attached to the rough endoplasmic reticulum and enters its lumen. Vesicles carry it to the Golgi complex, where it is modified and packed. Secretory vesicles then fuse with the plasma membrane and release it. Every organelle in this route is absent in a bacterium.
Why not the others: (A) This route uses no membrane-bound organelle, so it is not special to the pancreatic cell. (B) The protein enters the endoplasmic reticulum lumen before the Golgi complex, not after it. (D) Lysosomes digest materials; they are not a station on the secretory route.
Key point: Rough ER → Golgi → secretory vesicle → plasma membrane is the secretory route of eukaryotic cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Acid-soluble and acid-insoluble fractions of a tissue
questions.question: A living tissue is ground in trichloroacetic acid and filtered. The retentate (acid-insoluble fraction) contains proteins, nucleic acids and polysaccharides. It also contains lipids whose molecular mass is only about 750 Da. Which explanation, with its prediction, is correct?
options: A) Lipids are polymers of fatty acids joined by ester bonds, so they are true macromolecules; mild hydrolysis of the retentate will give long chains of fatty acid monomers
B) The acid joins lipids to proteins by covalent bonds; the lipids can be released only by breaking peptide bonds

C) Lipids are not polymers; membranes break into vesicles that are not water soluble and stay with the retentate; shaking the retentate with chloroform will remove the lipids without breaking any covalent bond
D) Lipids of this size always pass into the filtrate; the lipid found in the retentate must be a polysaccharide that was wrongly identified
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Lipids are not polymers; membranes break into vesicles that are not water soluble and stay with the retentate; shaking the retentate with chloroform will remove the lipids without breaking any covalent bond.
Concept: The acid-soluble pool has small molecules of about 18 to 800 Da. The acid-insoluble fraction has the macromolecules: proteins, nucleic acids and polysaccharides, with molecular mass above about 10,000 Da. Lipids are the exception: they are small but are found in the acid-insoluble fraction.
Why: Lipids are present in cells as parts of membranes. On grinding, membranes break into pieces and form vesicles that do not dissolve in water, so they are held back with the macromolecules. They are held together by non-covalent forces, so an organic solvent such as chloroform dissolves them out with no bond broken. This shows they are not polymers.
Why not the others: (A) A lipid such as a triglyceride or lecithin has a small fixed number of fatty acids on glycerol; it is not a long chain of repeating monomers. (B) The acid precipitates macromolecules; it does not form lipid–protein covalent bonds. (D) The retentate does contain lipids; their presence is explained by membrane vesicles, not by a wrong identification.
Key point: Lipids are in the macromolecular fraction because of membrane vesicles, not because they are polymers.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Levels of protein structure: unfolding and refolding
questions.question: An enzyme made of a single polypeptide chain loses all activity in concentrated urea. Analysis shows that no peptide bond is broken. When the urea is removed slowly, the enzyme regains full activity. Which conclusion is correct?
options: A) Urea disturbed the folded (secondary and tertiary) structure; the intact primary structure was enough to fold the chain correctly again
B) Urea changed the primary structure; removal of urea put the amino acids back in their original order
C) Urea disturbed only the quaternary structure, because this is the only level that affects activity
D) Urea hydrolysed the peptide bonds, and they formed again when it was removed
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Urea disturbed the folded (secondary and tertiary) structure; the intact primary structure was enough to fold the chain correctly again.
Concept: The primary structure of a protein is its amino acid sequence, held by peptide bonds. Secondary and tertiary structures are folds held mainly by weak bonds. The tertiary structure is necessary for the biological activity of a protein.
Why: No peptide bond was broken, so the sequence did not change. Activity was lost, so the three-dimensional fold was lost. Activity returned when urea was removed, so the unchanged sequence carried the information needed to fold again.
Why not the others: (B) The primary structure can change only if peptide bonds break and re-form, and none was broken. (C) A single polypeptide chain has no quaternary structure. (D) The analysis showed that no peptide bond was broken.
Key point: Sequence decides the fold, and the fold decides the activity.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: DNA content and chromosome number through the cell cycle
questions.question: Cells of a diploid organism have 2n = 8, and a cell in the G1 phase has 4 pg of DNA. A dividing culture is treated with a drug that prevents formation of spindle fibres but does not affect any other event. After some hours most cells are found stopped at one stage. What are the DNA content, number of chromosomes and number of chromatids in one such cell?
options: A) 4 pg, 8 chromosomes, 8 chromatids
B) 8 pg, 16 chromosomes, 16 chromatids
C) 4 pg, 4 chromosomes, 8 chromatids
D) 8 pg, 8 chromosomes, 16 chromatids
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 8 pg, 8 chromosomes, 16 chromatids.
Concept: DNA is replicated in the S phase, so the DNA content doubles from 2C to 4C, but the number of chromosomes does not change because the two sister chromatids stay joined at the centromere. Chromatids separate only in anaphase, and this needs spindle fibres.
Why: Without spindle fibres the cells pass through S and G2, enter mitosis and stop before anaphase, with condensed chromosomes that cannot be pulled apart. DNA content is double the G1 value: 2 × 4 pg = 8 pg. The centromeres have not split, so there are still 8 chromosomes, each with 2 chromatids: 8 × 2 = 16 chromatids.
Why not the others: (A) This is a G1 cell, before DNA replication. (B) 16 chromosomes would be seen only after the centromeres split in anaphase, which cannot happen without a spindle. (C) Four chromosomes with half the DNA would be a product of meiosis I, and the cell is dividing by mitosis.
Key point: S phase doubles DNA and chromatids, not chromosome number; anaphase doubles chromosome number.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Photosynthetic pigments: absorption and action spectrum
questions.question:
Pigments from spinach leaves were separated and their absorption peaks measured. The rate of photosynthesis of the intact leaf was then measured in light of different wavelengths.

Pigment | Absorption peaks (nm)
Chlorophyll a | 430 and 662
Chlorophyll b | 453 and 642
Carotenoids | 450 to 490

Wavelength (nm) | 430 | 480 | 550 | 662
Relative rate of photosynthesis | 90 | 70 | 15 | 100

Chlorophyll a absorbs very little light at 480 nm. What best explains the high rate at 480 nm?
options: A) The reaction centre chlorophyll a absorbs 480 nm light as well as it absorbs 662 nm light
B) Chlorophyll b and carotenoids absorb this light and pass the energy to chlorophyll a
C) Carotenoids reduce NADP+ directly, without chlorophyll a
D) Light of 480 nm is absorbed by water, which then splits and releases electrons
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Chlorophyll b and carotenoids absorb this light and pass the energy to chlorophyll a.
Concept: Chlorophyll a is the chief pigment that traps light for photosynthesis. Chlorophyll b, xanthophylls and carotenes are accessory pigments. They absorb light of other wavelengths and transfer the energy to chlorophyll a, so a wider range of light is used.
Why: The table shows that chlorophyll b (453 nm) and carotenoids (450 to 490 nm) absorb near 480 nm, where chlorophyll a absorbs little. The rate is still 70 at 480 nm, so the light absorbed by the accessory pigments is being used. The rate is low (15) at 550 nm, where no listed pigment absorbs.
Why not the others: (A) The stem and the table show that chlorophyll a has no peak at 480 nm. (C) Accessory pigments transfer energy to chlorophyll a; they do not carry out the reduction of NADP+ on their own. (D) Water is split by the complex associated with photosystem II using energy trapped by pigments; water does not absorb this light to split itself.
Key point: The action spectrum is wider than the absorption spectrum of chlorophyll a because of accessory pigments.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Alcoholic and lactic acid fermentation compared
questions.question: Yeast cells kept without oxygen convert glucose to ethanol. Skeletal muscle cells short of oxygen convert glucose to lactic acid. Which comparison of the two processes is correct?
options: A) Both reoxidise NADH to NAD+ and both give a net gain of 2 ATP per glucose; only the yeast pathway releases carbon dioxide
B) Both release carbon dioxide; only the muscle pathway reoxidises NADH to NAD+
C) The muscle pathway gives a net gain of 2 ATP per glucose, and the yeast pathway gives 4 ATP because it has one more step
D) Neither reoxidises NADH; both stop when the NAD+ of the cell is used up
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both reoxidise NADH to NAD+ and both give a net gain of 2 ATP per glucose; only the yeast pathway releases carbon dioxide.
Concept: In fermentation, glucose is partly oxidised by glycolysis to pyruvic acid, with a net gain of 2 ATP and 2 NADH. The NADH is then reoxidised to NAD+ while pyruvic acid is reduced, so that glycolysis can continue.
Why: In yeast, pyruvic acid is converted to carbon dioxide and ethanol by pyruvic acid decarboxylase and alcohol dehydrogenase. In muscle, pyruvic acid is reduced to lactic acid by lactate dehydrogenase, with no carbon dioxide released. In both, NADH is reoxidised to NAD+ and the only ATP comes from glycolysis: a net gain of 2 ATP per glucose.
Why not the others: (B) Lactic acid has three carbons, the same as pyruvic acid, so no carbon dioxide is released in muscle; and both pathways reoxidise NADH. (C) The steps after glycolysis make no ATP in either pathway. (D) Reoxidation of NADH is the purpose of the last step of both pathways.
Key point: Fermentation gives 2 ATP per glucose and regenerates NAD+; only alcoholic fermentation releases carbon dioxide.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Types of neurons by number of processes
questions.question: Neuron X has one axon and one dendrite. Neuron Y has one axon and several dendrites. Which statement about X and Y is correct?
options: A) X is unipolar and is found in the cerebral cortex; Y is bipolar and is found in the retina
B) X is multipolar and is found in the retina; Y is bipolar and is found in the cerebral cortex
C) X is bipolar, as in the retina of the eye; Y is multipolar, as in the cerebral cortex
D) X is bipolar, as in the cerebral cortex; Y is multipolar, as in the retina of the eye
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) X is bipolar, as in the retina of the eye; Y is multipolar, as in the cerebral cortex.
Concept: Neurons are of three types based on the number of axons and dendrites. A multipolar neuron has one axon and two or more dendrites and is found in the cerebral cortex. A bipolar neuron has one axon and one dendrite and is found in the retina of the eye. A unipolar neuron has a cell body with one axon only and is found usually in the embryonic stage.
Why: X has one axon and one dendrite, so it is bipolar. Y has one axon and several dendrites, so it is multipolar. Their typical locations are the retina and the cerebral cortex respectively.
Why not the others: (A) A unipolar neuron has an axon only, and X has a dendrite too; Y has several dendrites, so it is not bipolar. (B) The two names are interchanged. (D) The names are right but the locations are interchanged.
Key point: Count the processes: axon only = unipolar; one axon + one dendrite = bipolar; one axon + many dendrites = multipolar.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Segregation with a lethal genotype: a 2 : 1 ratio
questions.question: In mice, crosses between two yellow mice always give yellow and grey young in the ratio 2 : 1. Crosses between yellow and grey mice always give yellow and grey young in the ratio 1 : 1. Grey × grey gives only grey. Coat colour is controlled by one gene with two alleles. If yellow × yellow crosses produce 120 live young in total, what is expected?
options: A) 90 yellow and 30 grey; one-third of the yellow young are homozygous
B) 60 yellow and 60 grey; the two alleles are co-dominant
C) 80 yellow and 40 grey; half of the yellow young are homozygous
D) 80 yellow and 40 grey; all the yellow young are heterozygous, because embryos homozygous for the yellow allele do not survive
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 80 yellow and 40 grey; all the yellow young are heterozygous, because embryos homozygous for the yellow allele do not survive.
Concept: By the law of segregation, a cross of two heterozygotes (Yy × Yy) gives the genotypes YY : Yy : yy in the ratio 1 : 2 : 1. If one genotype does not survive, the ratio among the live young changes.
Why: Grey × grey gives only grey, so grey is the recessive homozygote yy. Yellow × grey always gives 1 : 1, so every yellow mouse tested is Yy; no true-breeding yellow mouse exists. Yy × Yy gives 1 YY : 2 Yy : 1 yy. The observed 2 yellow : 1 grey is obtained if the YY class is missing. Of 120 live young, yellow = 2/3 × 120 = 80, all Yy, and grey = 1/3 × 120 = 40.
Why not the others: (A) 90 : 30 is the 3 : 1 ratio, which is not observed; a homozygous yellow would give only yellow young with grey, which never happens. (B) Co-dominance would give a third phenotype, and 1 : 1 is the result of yellow × grey, not yellow × yellow. (C) The numbers are right, but a homozygous yellow mouse would not give the 1 : 1 ratio seen in every yellow × grey cross.
Key point: A 2 : 1 ratio from a cross of two heterozygotes means one homozygous class is lethal.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Dihybrid F2 ratio from counted seeds
questions.question:
Pea plants grown from round yellow seeds were self-pollinated, and the seeds they produced were counted.

Seed type | round yellow | round green | wrinkled yellow | wrinkled green
Number | 315 | 108 | 101 | 32

Round is dominant over wrinkled and yellow is dominant over green. Which conclusion is supported?
options: A) The ratio is close to 3 : 1; the parent plants were heterozygous for seed shape only
B) The ratio is close to 9 : 3 : 3 : 1; the parent plants were heterozygous for both genes, and about one-sixteenth of the seeds are homozygous recessive for both
C) The ratio is close to 1 : 1 : 1 : 1; the parent plants were crossed with a double recessive plant
D) The ratio is close to 9 : 7; the two genes control the same character
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The ratio is close to 9 : 3 : 3 : 1; the parent plants were heterozygous for both genes, and about one-sixteenth of the seeds are homozygous recessive for both.
Concept: When a plant heterozygous for two genes (RrYy) is self-pollinated and the genes assort independently, the offspring show four phenotypes in the ratio 9 : 3 : 3 : 1. The class that shows both recessive characters is 1/16 of the total and has the genotype rryy.
Why: The total is 315 + 108 + 101 + 32 = 556. One-sixteenth of 556 is about 35. So 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 predicts about 313 : 104 : 104 : 35, which is close to the counts. Four phenotypes from selfing means that both characters segregate, so the parent plants were RrYy. The 32 wrinkled green seeds are the rryy class, about 1/16 of the total.
Why not the others: (A) A 3 : 1 ratio has two classes only; here there are four, so seed colour segregates as well. (C) 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 would give about 139 in each class, and the plants were self-pollinated, not test-crossed. (D) 9 : 7 has two classes only, and the table has four classes for two different characters.
Key point: Selfing a double heterozygote gives 9 : 3 : 3 : 1, with 1/16 double recessive.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Hershey and Chase experiment: the role of blending
questions.question:
Bacteriophages labelled with 35S or with 32P were allowed to infect bacteria. The cultures were agitated in a blender and then centrifuged.

Label | Radioactivity in supernatant | Radioactivity in pellet (bacteria)
35S | 80% | 20%
32P | 30% | 70%

The experiment is repeated exactly, but the blender step is left out. What result is expected, and what follows?
options: A) Both labels are found mostly in the supernatant; the phage does not attach to bacteria without blending
B) Both labels are found mostly in the pellet; the experiment can no longer show which molecule entered the bacteria
C) 35S stays mostly in the supernatant and 32P mostly in the pellet, as before; blending has no role in the experiment
D) 32P is found mostly in the supernatant; DNA cannot enter the bacteria unless the culture is blended
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Both labels are found mostly in the pellet; the experiment can no longer show which molecule entered the bacteria.
Concept: In the Hershey and Chase experiment 35S labels the protein coat and 32P labels the DNA of the phage. The phage attaches to the bacterium and its DNA enters. Blending removes the empty viral coats from the bacterial surface. Centrifugation then sends the heavier bacteria to the pellet and leaves the lighter viral particles in the supernatant.
Why: Without blending, the protein coats stay attached to the bacterial surface. In centrifugation they go to the pellet together with the bacteria. So 35S (on the coats) and 32P (inside the cells) are both found mostly in the pellet. The pellet no longer separates "entered the cell" from "stuck outside the cell", so the experiment cannot identify the genetic material.
Why not the others: (A) Attachment happens before blending and does not need it; the 32P in the pellet shows that infection took place. (C) Blending is the step that moves 35S to the supernatant by shearing the coats off the cells. (D) DNA enters during infection, before the blending step.
Key point: Blending separates the coats outside from the DNA inside; this separation is what makes the two labels informative.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Base composition of double-stranded DNA and single-stranded RNA
questions.question:
The base composition (mole per cent) of two nucleic acid samples is given.

Sample | A | G | C | T | U
1 | 28 | 22 | 22 | 28 | 0
2 | 28 | 30 | 22 | 0 | 20

Which description of the two samples is consistent with these data?
options: A) Sample 1 is double-stranded DNA; sample 2 is single-stranded RNA
B) Sample 1 is single-stranded DNA; sample 2 is double-stranded RNA
C) Both samples are double-stranded DNA
D) Sample 1 is double-stranded DNA; sample 2 is double-stranded RNA
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Sample 1 is double-stranded DNA; sample 2 is single-stranded RNA.
Concept: DNA has thymine and RNA has uracil. In a double-stranded nucleic acid the bases pair, so the amounts of the paired bases are equal: A = T (or A = U) and G = C. A single-stranded molecule need not show these equalities.
Why: Sample 1 has T and no U, so it is DNA; A = T = 28 and G = C = 22, as expected for a double strand. Sample 2 has U and no T, so it is RNA; A (28) is not equal to U (20) and G (30) is not equal to C (22), so its bases are not all paired and it is single-stranded.
Why not the others: (B) Sample 1 obeys A = T and G = C, and sample 2 does not obey A = U and G = C; the two descriptions are interchanged. (C) Sample 2 has uracil and no thymine, so it is not DNA. (D) Double-stranded RNA would have A = U and G = C, which sample 2 does not have.
Key point: T or U tells DNA from RNA; equal amounts of paired bases point to a double strand.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Chemical evolution: what Miller's experiment does and does not show
questions.question:
Three closed flasks are set up as in S. L. Miller's experiment and run for a week at 800 °C.
Flask I: CH4, NH3, H2 and water vapour, with electric discharge.
Flask II: the same gases with free O2 added, with electric discharge.
Flask III: the same gases as flask I at the same temperature, with no electric discharge.
Amino acids are found in flask I only. Consider these statements.
(i) Under these conditions the electric discharge is needed for the formation of amino acids from these gases.
(ii) The result of flask II agrees with the idea that the atmosphere in which the first organic molecules formed was a reducing one.
(iii) The result of flask I disproves Pasteur's conclusion that life comes only from pre-existing life.
(iv) The result of flask I shows how the first cells were formed.
Which statements are supported?
options: A) (i), (ii) and (iii) only
B) (i) and (iv) only
C) (ii) and (iii) only
D) (i) and (ii) only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (i) and (ii) only.
Concept: Oparin and Haldane proposed that the first form of life could have come from non-living organic molecules, and that formation of life was preceded by chemical evolution. Miller created electric discharge in a closed flask containing CH4, H2, NH3 and water vapour at 800 °C and observed the formation of amino acids. Pasteur showed that life comes only from pre-existing life in sterilised flasks.
Why: Flask I and flask III differ only in the electric discharge, and only flask I gives amino acids, so (i) is supported. Flask I and flask II differ only in free oxygen, and amino acids are found only without it, so (ii) is supported. Amino acids are molecules, not living organisms. Their formation says nothing against Pasteur's result on organisms, so (iii) is not supported, and it does not show how cells arose, so (iv) is not supported.
Why not the others: (A) It includes (iii); making an organic molecule is not the same as producing a living organism from non-living matter. (B) It includes (iv); the experiment stops at small organic molecules and does not show the formation of cells. (C) It includes (iii) and leaves out (i), which follows from comparing flasks I and III.
Key point: Miller's experiment supports chemical evolution of organic molecules; it does not show spontaneous generation of organisms.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Typhoid and common cold: cause, test and treatment
questions.question: Patient 1 has had sustained fever of 39 to 40 °C for a week, with weakness, stomach pain, constipation, headache and loss of appetite, and the Widal test is positive. Patient 2 has a blocked nose, sore throat, cough and headache for three days. Both ask for an antibiotic. Which assessment is correct?
options: A) Patient 1 has pneumonia caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae; an antibiotic will help both patients
B) Both patients have bacterial infections of the intestine; an antibiotic will help both
C) Patient 1 has typhoid caused by Salmonella typhi, and an antibiotic is appropriate; patient 2 has common cold caused by rhinoviruses, and an antibiotic will not act on the virus
D) Patient 1 has malaria caused by Plasmodium; patient 2 has typhoid; an antibiotic is appropriate only for patient 2
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Patient 1 has typhoid caused by Salmonella typhi, and an antibiotic is appropriate; patient 2 has common cold caused by rhinoviruses, and an antibiotic will not act on the virus.
Concept: Typhoid is caused by the bacterium Salmonella typhi. Its symptoms are sustained high fever (39 to 40 °C), weakness, stomach pain, constipation, headache and loss of appetite, and it is confirmed by the Widal test. Common cold is caused by rhinoviruses, which infect the nose and respiratory passage but not the lungs. Antibiotics act on bacteria, not on viruses.
Why: The symptoms and the positive Widal test of patient 1 match typhoid, a bacterial disease, so an antibiotic is appropriate. The symptoms of patient 2 match common cold, a viral disease, so an antibiotic has no action on its cause.
Why not the others: (A) Pneumonia affects the alveoli and gives fever, chills, cough and difficulty in breathing; the Widal test is for typhoid. (B) Patient 2 has a viral infection of the nose and respiratory passage, not a bacterial infection of the intestine. (D) Malaria gives chills and high fever recurring every three to four days, and the Widal test does not detect it; patient 2 has no sign of typhoid.
Key point: Widal test → typhoid (bacterial); rhinovirus → common cold (viral); antibiotics do not act on viruses.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Making recombinant DNA with a restriction enzyme and ligase
questions.question: A gene is to be inserted into a plasmid using EcoRI and DNA ligase. Which order of steps will give recombinant plasmids?
options: A) Cut the plasmid and the donor DNA with EcoRI → mix them so that the sticky ends pair → add DNA ligase → introduce the DNA into host cells
B) Add DNA ligase to the uncut plasmid and donor DNA → cut with EcoRI → introduce the DNA into host cells
C) Cut only the donor DNA with EcoRI → mix with uncut plasmid → add DNA ligase → introduce the DNA into host cells
D) Cut the plasmid and the donor DNA with EcoRI → introduce the pieces into host cells → add DNA ligase to the culture medium
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Cut the plasmid and the donor DNA with EcoRI → mix them so that the sticky ends pair → add DNA ligase → introduce the DNA into host cells.
Concept: A restriction endonuclease cuts DNA at its specific recognition sequence and leaves single-stranded overhangs called sticky ends. DNA pieces cut by the same enzyme have the same sticky ends, which can pair by hydrogen bonds. DNA ligase then joins the sugar-phosphate backbones.
Why: Both the plasmid and the donor DNA must be cut with the same enzyme so that their ends are complementary. On mixing, the ends of the gene pair with the ends of the opened plasmid. Ligase seals the nicks and gives a stable recombinant plasmid, which is then introduced into the host.
Why not the others: (B) Ligase has no free ends to join in uncut DNA, and cutting afterwards only opens the molecules again. (C) An uncut circular plasmid has no free sticky ends, so the gene cannot be inserted into it. (D) Ligase added to the medium does not join the pieces before they enter the cells; the joining must be done before transformation.
Key point: Same enzyme for vector and insert → complementary sticky ends → ligase → transformation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Birth rate, death rate, immigration and emigration
questions.question: A pond had 400 fish at the start of a year. During the year there were 160 births and 80 deaths; 20 fish entered from a connected stream and 40 fish left through it. What are the per capita birth rate, the per capita death rate and the number of fish at the end of the year?
options: A) 0.4 per fish per year; 0.2 per fish per year; 480
B) 160 per fish per year; 80 per fish per year; 460
C) 0.4 per fish per year; 0.2 per fish per year; 460
D) 0.35 per fish per year; 0.17 per fish per year; 460
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 0.4 per fish per year; 0.2 per fish per year; 460.
Concept: Birth rate and death rate of a population are expressed per individual (per capita). Population density changes by natality and immigration, which add individuals, and mortality and emigration, which remove them.
Given: \(N_0=400,\ B=160,\ D=80,\ I=20,\ E=40\) in one year.
Formula/Principle: \(b=\dfrac{B}{N_0},\quad d=\dfrac{D}{N_0},\quad N_1=N_0+(B+I)-(D+E)\)
Step 1: \(b=\dfrac{160}{400}=0.4\) per fish per year.
Step 2: \(d=\dfrac{80}{400}=0.2\) per fish per year.
Step 3: \[N_1=400+(160+20)-(80+40)=400+180-120=460\]
Why: The rates are found by dividing by the population at the start, and all four processes are counted in the final number.
Why not the others: (A) 480 = 400 + 160 − 80 leaves out immigration and emigration. (B) 160 and 80 are total births and deaths, not per capita rates. (D) 0.35 and 0.17 are obtained by dividing by the final number 460 instead of the starting number 400.
Key point: N(t+1) = N(t) + [(B + I) − (D + E)].

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Stratification in an ecosystem
questions.question:
Light reaching different layers of a forest was measured at noon.

Layer | Height above ground | Light received (per cent of full sunlight)
Trees | 20 to 30 m | 100
Shrubs | 2 to 5 m | 15
Herbs and grasses | below 1 m | 3

Which conclusion is best supported by these data?
options: A) The herb layer has the highest primary productivity per unit area, because it is nearest to the soil
B) The species are arranged in vertical layers, and the plants of the lower layers must be able to grow in weak light
C) Decomposition cannot take place below the shrub layer, because very little light reaches it
D) The data form an inverted pyramid of energy for the forest
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The species are arranged in vertical layers, and the plants of the lower layers must be able to grow in weak light.
Concept: Vertical distribution of different species occupying different levels is called stratification. In a forest, trees occupy the top layer, shrubs the second, and herbs and grasses the bottom layers.
Why: The table shows three layers at different heights. Light falls from 100 per cent at the tree layer to 15 per cent at the shrub layer and 3 per cent at the herb layer. So the layers differ in the light they get, and herbs and grasses of the forest floor are plants that can grow in weak light.
Why not the others: (A) Productivity depends on light captured, and the herb layer gets only 3 per cent of full sunlight. (C) Decomposition is carried out by decomposers acting on detritus and does not need light. (D) A pyramid of energy compares trophic levels, not layers of plants, and it is never inverted.
Key point: Stratification is the vertical layering of species in an ecosystem.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Species–area relationship: effect of the slope Z
questions.question: The species–area relationship is log S = log C + Z log A. A survey of patches inside one region gave Z = 0.15. A survey of very large areas, such as whole continents, gave Z = 1.0. If the area sampled is increased 100 times in each survey, by what factor does species richness increase? (10^0.3 ≈ 2)
options: A) About 15 times in the first survey and 100 times in the second
B) About 2 times in both surveys
C) About 100 times in the first survey and 2 times in the second
D) About 2 times in the first survey and 100 times in the second
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) About 2 times in the first survey and 100 times in the second.
Concept: Alexander von Humboldt observed that species richness increases with explored area, but only up to a limit. The relation is S = C A^Z, a straight line on a log scale with slope Z. Z is 0.1 to 0.2 for small areas inside a region and 0.6 to 1.2 for very large areas such as whole continents.
Given: \(S=CA^{Z};\ \dfrac{A_2}{A_1}=100;\ Z_1=0.15,\ Z_2=1.0\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{S_2}{S_1}=\left(\dfrac{A_2}{A_1}\right)^{Z}\)
Step 1: \(\left(100\right)^{0.15}=\left(10^{2}\right)^{0.15}=10^{0.3}\approx 2\)
Step 2: \[\left(100\right)^{1.0}=100\]
Why: The same increase in area gives a much larger increase in species when the slope Z is steeper.
Why not the others: (A) 15 comes from multiplying 100 by 0.15; Z is an exponent, not a multiplier. (B) The second survey has Z = 1.0, which gives 100 times, not 2 times. (C) The two surveys are interchanged.
Key point: S = C A^Z; Z is about 0.1 to 0.2 within a region and 0.6 to 1.2 across continents.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Law of multiple proportions from combining masses
questions.question: Copper forms two oxides. In oxide P, 1.00 g of oxygen is combined with 3.97 g of copper. In oxide Q, 1.00 g of oxygen is combined with 7.94 g of copper. The formula of P is CuO. Which law do these data illustrate, and what is the formula of Q?
options: A) Law of definite proportions; \(\ce{CuO2}\)
B) Law of multiple proportions; \(\ce{CuO2}\)
C) Law of multiple proportions; \(\ce{Cu2O}\)
D) Law of conservation of mass; \(\ce{Cu2O}\)
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Law of multiple proportions; \(\ce{Cu2O}\).
Concept: Law of multiple proportions (Dalton): if two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a ratio of small whole numbers.
Why: For a fixed mass of oxygen (1.00 g), the masses of copper are 3.97 g and 7.94 g. Their ratio is \(3.97:7.94=1:2\), a simple whole-number ratio, which is the law of multiple proportions. Q has twice as much copper per oxygen atom as P. Since P is CuO, Q is \(\ce{Cu2O}\).
Why not the others: (A) The law of definite proportions is about one compound always having the same composition; here two different compounds are compared, and \(\ce{CuO2}\) would have half the copper per oxygen, not double. (B) The law is right, but \(\ce{CuO2}\) has less copper per oxygen than CuO, while Q has more. (D) Conservation of mass compares the mass before and after a reaction, which is not given here.
Key point: Fix the mass of one element; a simple ratio of the masses of the other shows multiple proportions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Isotopic abundance and number of neutrons in a sample
questions.question: An element X (Z = 29) has two isotopes with mass numbers 63 and 65. Its average atomic mass is 63.5 u. Take the mass of each isotope in u as equal to its mass number and \(N_A=6.0\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}\). What is the percentage of the lighter isotope, and how many neutrons are there in 0.10 mol of atoms of X?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 75%; \(2.1\times10^{24}\).
Concept: Isotopes have the same atomic number and different mass numbers. The average atomic mass is the abundance-weighted mean of the isotopic masses. Number of neutrons = mass number − atomic number.
Given: \(Z=29;\ A=63,\ 65;\ \bar A=63.5\ \mathrm u;\ n=0.10\ \mathrm{mol};\ N_A=6.0\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\bar A=63x+65(1-x);\quad \text{average neutrons per atom}=\bar A-Z\)
Step 1: \(63x+65-65x=63.5\Rightarrow 2x=1.5\Rightarrow x=0.75\ (75\%)\)
Step 2: \(\bar A-Z=63.5-29=34.5\) neutrons per atom on average.
Step 3: \[N=0.10\times6.0\times10^{23}\times34.5=2.07\times10^{24}\approx2.1\times10^{24}\]
Why: The average mass 63.5 is nearer to 63 than to 65, so the lighter isotope is the more abundant one.
Why not the others: (B) 25% is the abundance of the heavier isotope. (C) \(3.8\times10^{24}\) uses 63.5 nucleons per atom instead of 34.5 neutrons. (D) Equal abundance would give an average mass of 64 u, not 63.5 u.
Key point: Average atomic mass = Σ(fraction × isotopic mass); neutrons = A − Z.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Classification of Elements and Periodicity; s and p block trends
questions.sub_topic: IUPAC systematic names for elements with Z > 100 and position in the periodic table
questions.question: An element with atomic number 119 has not yet been made. Element 118 completes the seventh period. Using the IUPAC systematic nomenclature for elements with Z > 100, what are the name, symbol and position of element 119?
options: A) Ununennium, Uue; group 18, period 7
B) Unnilennium, Une; group 1, period 8
C) Ununoctium, Uuo; group 1, period 8
D) Ununennium, Uue; group 1, period 8
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Ununennium, Uue; group 1, period 8.
Concept: The IUPAC systematic name is built from numerical roots for the digits of the atomic number (0 nil, 1 un, 2 bi, 3 tri, 4 quad, 5 pent, 6 hex, 7 sept, 8 oct, 9 enn) followed by "ium". The symbol is made of the first letters of the roots. An element that follows a noble gas starts a new period in group 1.
Why: 119 has the digits 1, 1, 9: un + un + enn + ium = ununennium, symbol Uue. Element 118 is the noble gas that ends period 7 with the configuration \(7s^27p^6\). The next electron enters 8s, so element 119 has \(8s^1\) as its outer configuration and is placed in group 1 of period 8.
Why not the others: (A) The name is right, but period 7 is already complete at element 118, so 119 cannot be in it. (B) Unnilennium (Une) is 1, 0, 9, that is element 109. (C) Ununoctium (Uuo) is 1, 1, 8, that is element 118.
Key point: Read the digits as roots, add "ium"; the element after a noble gas is an s-block element of the next period.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Lattice enthalpy of ionic solids: charge and size
questions.question: Consider the ionic solids NaF, NaCl, MgO and CaO, all with the same crystal structure. Which is the correct order of lattice enthalpy, with the main reason?
options: A) NaF > NaCl > MgO > CaO; singly charged ions pack more closely
B) MgO > CaO > NaF > NaCl; the product of ionic charges matters most, and for equal charges the smaller interionic distance gives the larger value
C) CaO > MgO > NaCl > NaF; larger ions have more electrons and attract more strongly
D) MgO > NaF > CaO > NaCl; only the interionic distance matters
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) MgO > CaO > NaF > NaCl; the product of ionic charges matters most, and for equal charges the smaller interionic distance gives the larger value.
Concept: Lattice enthalpy is the enthalpy needed to separate one mole of an ionic solid into gaseous ions. The attraction between ions follows Coulomb's law, so it rises with the product of the charges and falls as the distance between the ions increases.
Why: MgO and CaO have ions of charge 2+ and 2−, so the charge product is 4. NaF and NaCl have 1+ and 1−, product 1. So both oxides are above both sodium halides. Within the oxides, \(\ce{Mg^2+}\) is smaller than \(\ce{Ca^2+}\), so MgO > CaO. Within the halides, \(\ce{F-}\) is smaller than \(\ce{Cl-}\), so NaF > NaCl.
Why not the others: (A) It puts the singly charged solids above the doubly charged ones, against Coulomb's law. (C) It reverses the size effect: larger ions are farther apart and attract less. (D) It ignores charge: CaO (charge product 4) has a much larger lattice enthalpy than NaF (charge product 1).
Key point: Lattice enthalpy increases with ionic charge and decreases with ionic size.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Sign of heat, work and internal energy change in an adiabatic compression
questions.question: A gas is held in a cylinder with thermally insulating walls and an insulating piston. The piston is pushed in quickly, and a thermometer in the gas shows a rise in temperature. Taking the gas as the system and using the IUPAC sign convention (work done on the system is positive), which set is correct?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(q=0,\ w>0,\ \Delta U>0\).
Concept: First law of thermodynamics: \(\Delta U=q+w\). A system that cannot exchange heat with the surroundings undergoes an adiabatic change, for which \(q=0\). Internal energy is a state function; for a gas it rises when the temperature rises.
Why: The walls and piston are insulating, so \(q=0\). The surroundings push the piston in, so work is done on the gas and \(w>0\). Then \(\Delta U=q+w=w>0\), which agrees with the observed rise in temperature.
Why not the others: (B) No heat can enter through insulating walls, and the volume changes, so work is not zero. (C) \(w<0\) is for an expansion, in which the gas would cool. (D) Heat cannot leave through insulating walls, and the temperature rise shows that \(\Delta U\) is not zero.
Key point: Adiabatic compression: q = 0 and ΔU = w > 0, so the gas warms.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Kp from total pressure and its use at a different starting pressure
questions.question:
For \(\ce{N2O4(g) <=> 2NO2(g)}\) at a fixed temperature, two experiments are done in rigid vessels, each starting with pure \(\ce{N2O4}\).

Experiment | Initial pressure of \(\ce{N2O4}\) (bar) | Total pressure at equilibrium (bar)
1 | 1.00 | 1.20
2 | 0.10 | ?

What are \(K_p\), the total pressure at equilibrium in experiment 2, and the change in the fraction of \(\ce{N2O4}\) dissociated from experiment 1 to experiment 2?
options: A) 0.20 bar; 0.12 bar; 20% in both experiments
B) 0.050 bar; 0.15 bar; 20% rises to 50%
C) 0.20 bar; 0.20 bar; 20% rises to 100%
D) 0.20 bar; 0.15 bar; 20% rises to 50%
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 0.20 bar; 0.15 bar; 20% rises to 50%.
Concept: For a gaseous equilibrium \(K_p\) is written with equilibrium partial pressures and depends only on temperature. If \(x\) bar of \(\ce{N2O4}\) dissociates, \(2x\) bar of \(\ce{NO2}\) forms, so the total pressure rises by \(x\).
Given: Experiment 1: \(p_0=1.00\) bar, \(p_{total}=1.20\) bar. Experiment 2: \(p_0=0.10\) bar.
Formula/Principle: \(K_p=\dfrac{p_{\ce{NO2}}^2}{p_{\ce{N2O4}}}=\dfrac{(2x)^2}{p_0-x};\quad p_{total}=p_0+x\)
Step 1: Experiment 1: \(1.00+x=1.20\Rightarrow x=0.20\) bar; fraction dissociated \(=0.20/1.00=20\%\).
Step 2: \(K_p=\dfrac{(0.40)^2}{0.80}=0.20\) bar.
Step 3: Experiment 2: \(\dfrac{4x^2}{0.10-x}=0.20\Rightarrow4x^2+0.20x-0.020=0\Rightarrow x=\dfrac{-0.20+\sqrt{0.04+0.32}}{8}=\dfrac{-0.20+0.60}{8}=0.050\) bar.
Step 4: \[p_{total}=0.10+0.050=0.15\ \text{bar};\qquad\text{fraction dissociated}=\frac{0.050}{0.10}=50\%\]
Why: \(K_p\) is the same in both experiments, but at the lower pressure the equilibrium lies further towards the side with more moles of gas, so a larger fraction dissociates.
Why not the others: (A) A fixed 20% in experiment 2 would give \(Q=(0.04)^2/0.08=0.020\) bar, not 0.20 bar. (B) 0.050 bar comes from using \(x^2/(p_0-x)\), which forgets that 2 mol of \(\ce{NO2}\) form per mol of \(\ce{N2O4}\). (C) Complete dissociation would leave no \(\ce{N2O4}\), which is not possible with a finite \(K_p\).
Key point: Kp is fixed at a given temperature; lowering the pressure increases the degree of dissociation when the number of moles of gas increases.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Le Chatelier's principle: temperature and addition of an inert gas at constant volume
questions.question: For \(\ce{N2(g) + 3H2(g) <=> 2NH3(g)}\), \(\Delta H<0\). The mixture is at equilibrium in a rigid vessel. Change 1: the temperature is raised. Change 2 (done separately): argon is added at constant volume and temperature. What happens?
options: A) Change 1 increases K and the amount of ammonia; change 2 has no effect
B) Change 1 decreases K and the amount of ammonia; change 2 shifts the equilibrium towards ammonia
C) Change 1 decreases K and the amount of ammonia; change 2 does not shift the equilibrium
D) Change 1 does not change K; change 2 shifts the equilibrium towards nitrogen and hydrogen
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Change 1 decreases K and the amount of ammonia; change 2 does not shift the equilibrium.
Concept: Le Chatelier's principle: a system at equilibrium shifts so as to reduce the effect of a change. The equilibrium constant changes only with temperature. For an exothermic reaction K decreases when the temperature is raised. An inert gas added at constant volume does not change the partial pressures or concentrations of the reacting gases.
Why: The forward reaction gives out heat. Raising the temperature favours the reverse (heat-absorbing) direction, so K and the amount of ammonia decrease. Argon at constant volume raises the total pressure, but the concentrations of \(\ce{N2}\), \(\ce{H2}\) and \(\ce{NH3}\) stay the same, so the reaction quotient still equals K and nothing shifts.
Why not the others: (A) K of an exothermic reaction falls, not rises, with temperature. (B) The first part is right, but argon at constant volume changes no concentration, so there is no shift. (D) K does change with temperature, and argon at constant volume causes no shift.
Key point: Only temperature changes K; an inert gas at constant volume has no effect on the equilibrium.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Average oxidation number of sulphur in thiosulphate and tetrathionate
questions.question: In an iodine titration, \(\ce{2S2O3^2- + I2 -> S4O6^2- + 2I-}\). What is the change in the average oxidation number of sulphur, and how many electrons does each thiosulphate ion lose?
options: A) +2 to +2.5; two electrons
B) +2 to +2.5; one electron
C) +4 to +5; one electron
D) +2 to +3; two electrons
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) +2 to +2.5; one electron.
Concept: The sum of the oxidation numbers of all atoms in an ion equals the charge of the ion, with oxygen taken as −2. When atoms of one element in a species are not all equivalent, this gives the average oxidation number. Loss of electrons is oxidation.
Why: In \(\ce{S2O3^2-}\): \(2x+3(-2)=-2\Rightarrow x=+2\). In \(\ce{S4O6^2-}\): \(4x+6(-2)=-2\Rightarrow x=+2.5\). Each sulphur atom rises by 0.5, and a thiosulphate ion has two sulphur atoms, so it loses \(2\times0.5=1\) electron. Check with iodine: \(\ce{I2}\) gains 2 electrons, and 2 thiosulphate ions supply them.
Why not the others: (A) Two electrons per thiosulphate would need \(\ce{2I2}\) for two thiosulphate ions, not one. (C) +4 and +5 are obtained if the charge on the ions is ignored or oxygen is miscounted. (D) +3 would give \(4(3)-12=0\), not the charge −2 of the tetrathionate ion.
Key point: Average oxidation number = (charge on ion − sum for other atoms) ÷ number of atoms of the element.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry: Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.sub_topic: IUPAC name of a branched alkane: longest chain and lowest locants
questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of \(\ce{CH3-CH(C2H5)-CH2-CH(CH3)-CH3}\), and what is the reason?
options: A) 2-Ethyl-4-methylpentane; the chain written in a straight line is the parent chain
B) 2,4-Dimethylhexane; the longest chain has six carbon atoms and the substituents get the lowest set of locants
C) 3,5-Dimethylhexane; the longest chain has six carbon atoms and is numbered from the ethyl end
D) 4-Ethyl-2-methylpentane; substituents are numbered in alphabetical order
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 2,4-Dimethylhexane; the longest chain has six carbon atoms and the substituents get the lowest set of locants.
Concept: IUPAC rules for alkanes: choose the longest continuous carbon chain as the parent, whichever way it is drawn; number it from the end that gives the substituents the lowest set of locants.
Why: The ethyl group written as a branch continues the chain. Going through it gives \(\ce{CH3-CH2-CH(CH3)-CH2-CH(CH3)-CH3}\), a chain of six carbon atoms (hexane) with two methyl groups. Numbering from the right gives locants 2 and 4; numbering from the left gives 3 and 5. The set (2, 4) is lower, so the name is 2,4-dimethylhexane.
Why not the others: (A) A five-carbon parent is not the longest chain; an ethyl group on C-2 always extends the chain. (C) The parent is right, but (3, 5) is a higher set of locants than (2, 4). (D) The parent chain is not the longest, and alphabetical order decides the order of writing the names, not the numbering.
Key point: Find the longest chain first, then give the lowest locants.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Free-radical monochlorination: number of products and their proportions
questions.question: 2-Methylbutane is chlorinated in sunlight to give monochloro products. At the temperature used, the relative reactivity per hydrogen atom is primary : secondary : tertiary = 1 : 4 : 5. How many constitutional isomers of formula \(\ce{C5H11Cl}\) are formed, and which is the major one, with its percentage?
options: A) 4; 2-chloro-2-methylbutane, about 42%
B) 3; 2-chloro-3-methylbutane, about 36%
C) 4; 1-chloro-2-methylbutane, about 50%
D) 4; 2-chloro-3-methylbutane, about 36%
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 4; 2-chloro-3-methylbutane, about 36%.
Concept: In free-radical halogenation of an alkane a chlorine atom abstracts a hydrogen atom. The amount of each product is proportional to (number of equivalent hydrogen atoms) × (reactivity of that kind of hydrogen). Tertiary hydrogen is the most reactive because the tertiary radical is the most stable.
Given: \(\ce{(CH3)2CH-CH2-CH3}\); reactivity per H: 1° = 1, 2° = 4, 3° = 5.
Formula/Principle: relative amount = number of H × reactivity; percentage = amount ÷ total × 100.
Step 1: Kinds of hydrogen: six 1° H on the two \(\ce{CH3}\) groups on C-2 → 1-chloro-2-methylbutane; one 3° H on C-2 → 2-chloro-2-methylbutane; two 2° H on C-3 → 2-chloro-3-methylbutane; three 1° H on C-4 → 1-chloro-3-methylbutane. So there are 4 constitutional isomers.
Step 2: Relative amounts: \(6\times1=6;\ 1\times5=5;\ 2\times4=8;\ 3\times1=3\). Total \(=22\).
Step 3: \[\%\ \text{of 2-chloro-3-methylbutane}=\frac{8}{22}\times100\approx36\%\]
Why: The two secondary hydrogens are fewer than the six primary ones, but each is four times as reactive, so their product is the largest share.
Why not the others: (A) The tertiary product is \(5/22\approx23\%\); 42% comes from dividing 5 by 12, the number of hydrogen atoms. (B) The percentage is right, but the two kinds of primary hydrogen give two different products, so there are 4 isomers, not 3. (C) 50% is 6/12, which counts hydrogen atoms and ignores their different reactivity; the correct share is \(6/22\approx27\%\).
Key point: Product share = number of equivalent H × relative reactivity.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Molality and molarity of a solution and the effect of temperature on each
questions.question: A solution contains 4.0 g of NaOH (molar mass 40 g mol⁻¹) in 96 g of water. Its density at 298 K is 1.04 g mL⁻¹. The solution is warmed to 318 K in a closed flask, and its volume increases. What are its molality and molarity at 298 K, and how do they change on warming?
options: A) 1.04 mol kg⁻¹ and 1.04 mol L⁻¹; the molality does not change and the molarity decreases
B) 1.04 mol kg⁻¹ and 1.04 mol L⁻¹; neither changes
C) 1.04 mol kg⁻¹ and 1.04 mol L⁻¹; the molality decreases and the molarity does not change
D) 1.00 mol kg⁻¹ and 1.04 mol L⁻¹; both increase
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 1.04 mol kg⁻¹ and 1.04 mol L⁻¹; the molality does not change and the molarity decreases.
Concept: Molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent. Molarity is moles of solute per litre of solution. Mass does not change with temperature, but volume does.
Given: \(m_{\ce{NaOH}}=4.0\) g; \(M=40\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}\); \(m_{water}=96\) g; \(\rho=1.04\ \mathrm{g\,mL^{-1}}\).
Formula/Principle: \(\text{molality}=\dfrac{n}{m_{solvent}(\mathrm{kg})};\quad\text{molarity}=\dfrac{n}{V_{solution}(\mathrm L)};\quad V=\dfrac{m_{solution}}{\rho}\)
Step 1: \(n=\dfrac{4.0}{40}=0.10\) mol.
Step 2: Molality \(=\dfrac{0.10}{0.096}=1.04\ \mathrm{mol\,kg^{-1}}\).
Step 3: \(V=\dfrac{100}{1.04}=96.2\) mL \(=0.0962\) L.
Step 4: \[\text{Molarity}=\frac{0.10}{0.0962}=1.04\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}}\]
Why: On warming, the masses of solute and solvent are unchanged, so the molality stays the same. The volume of the solution increases, so the molarity (moles per litre) decreases.
Why not the others: (B) Molarity depends on volume, which increases on warming. (C) The two effects are interchanged: molality is based on mass and cannot change. (D) 1.00 mol kg⁻¹ is obtained by dividing by 100 g of solution instead of 96 g of solvent, and neither quantity increases on warming.
Key point: Molality is independent of temperature; molarity decreases as the solution expands.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Standard electrode potentials: reducing power and cell emf
questions.question: Standard reduction potentials: \(\ce{Zn^2+/Zn}=-0.76\) V, \(\ce{Fe^2+/Fe}=-0.44\) V, \(\ce{Cu^2+/Cu}=+0.34\) V, \(\ce{Ag+/Ag}=+0.80\) V. Which is the correct order of reducing power of the metals, and which pair of these electrodes gives the galvanic cell of highest standard emf?
options: A) Ag > Cu > Fe > Zn; zinc and silver, 1.56 V
B) Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag; zinc and silver, 0.04 V
C) Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag; zinc and silver, 1.56 V
D) Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag; zinc and copper, 1.10 V
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag; zinc and silver, 1.56 V.
Concept: A lower (more negative) standard reduction potential means the metal ion is harder to reduce, so the metal is more easily oxidised and is a stronger reducing agent. \(E^\circ_{cell}=E^\circ_{cathode}-E^\circ_{anode}\), with both written as reduction potentials.
Why: The reduction potentials increase in the order Zn (−0.76) < Fe (−0.44) < Cu (+0.34) < Ag (+0.80), so the reducing power decreases in the order Zn > Fe > Cu > Ag. The largest emf is obtained from the two electrodes farthest apart: \(E^\circ_{cell}=0.80-(-0.76)=1.56\) V, with zinc as the anode and silver as the cathode.
Why not the others: (A) This is the order of oxidising power of the ions, reversed for the metals. (B) 0.04 V comes from adding 0.80 and −0.76 instead of subtracting. (D) The order is right, but the zinc–copper cell gives 1.10 V, which is less than 1.56 V.
Key point: Lower E° means stronger reducing agent; E°cell = E°cathode − E°anode.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Average rate of reaction and rate of formation of a product
questions.question: For \(\ce{2N2O5(g) -> 4NO2(g) + O2(g)}\) in a closed vessel, the concentration of \(\ce{N2O5}\) falls from 0.100 mol L⁻¹ to 0.080 mol L⁻¹ in 100 s. What are the average rate of the reaction and the average rate of formation of \(\ce{NO2}\) in this interval?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) \(1.0\times10^{-4}\) and \(4.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,s^{-1}}\).
Concept: The rate of a reaction is the rate of change of concentration of any reactant or product divided by its stoichiometric coefficient, so that it has one value for the reaction.
Given: \(\Delta[\ce{N2O5}]=0.080-0.100=-0.020\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}};\ \Delta t=100\) s.
Formula/Principle: \(\text{rate}=-\dfrac12\dfrac{\Delta[\ce{N2O5}]}{\Delta t}=\dfrac14\dfrac{\Delta[\ce{NO2}]}{\Delta t}=\dfrac{\Delta[\ce{O2}]}{\Delta t}\)
Step 1: \(-\dfrac{\Delta[\ce{N2O5}]}{\Delta t}=\dfrac{0.020}{100}=2.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,s^{-1}}\).
Step 2: Rate of reaction \(=\dfrac12\times2.0\times10^{-4}=1.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,s^{-1}}\).
Step 3: \[\frac{\Delta[\ce{NO2}]}{\Delta t}=4\times1.0\times10^{-4}=4.0\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mol\,L^{-1}\,s^{-1}}\]
Why: Two moles of \(\ce{N2O5}\) give four moles of \(\ce{NO2}\), so \(\ce{NO2}\) forms twice as fast as \(\ce{N2O5}\) disappears.
Why not the others: (A) \(2.0\times10^{-4}\) is the rate of disappearance of \(\ce{N2O5}\), not the rate of reaction. (B) \(2.0\times10^{-4}\) is the rate of disappearance of \(\ce{N2O5}\), not the rate of formation of \(\ce{NO2}\). (C) Both values are double the correct ones because the coefficient 2 of \(\ce{N2O5}\) is not used.
Key point: Rate = (1/coefficient) × rate of change of concentration.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Highest oxidation states of the 3d metals and the outer configuration
questions.question:
The table gives the outer electronic configuration and the highest oxidation state known for some 3d metals.

Metal | Sc | Ti | V | Cr | Mn | Fe | Ni | Zn
Outer configuration | \(3d^14s^2\) | \(3d^24s^2\) | \(3d^34s^2\) | \(3d^54s^1\) | \(3d^54s^2\) | \(3d^64s^2\) | \(3d^84s^2\) | \(3d^{10}4s^2\)
Highest oxidation state | +3 | +4 | +5 | +6 | +7 | +6 | +4 | +2

What best explains the rise up to manganese and the fall after it?
options: A) Up to Mn the highest state equals the total number of 4s and 3d electrons; after Mn the d electrons begin to pair, so fewer are available for bonding
B) The lanthanoid contraction makes the atoms after Mn too small to reach high oxidation states
C) After Mn the 4s electrons are no longer used in bonding, so only the 3d electrons count
D) The ionisation enthalpies fall steadily after Mn, so the atoms lose fewer electrons
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Up to Mn the highest state equals the total number of 4s and 3d electrons; after Mn the d electrons begin to pair, so fewer are available for bonding.
Concept: Transition metals show variable oxidation states because the 3d and 4s electrons are close in energy and both take part in bonding. The highest states are reached in oxides and fluorides.
Why: From the table, Sc (3 outer electrons) shows +3, Ti (4) shows +4, V (5) shows +5, Cr (6) shows +6 and Mn (7) shows +7. So up to Mn all the 4s and 3d electrons are used. Beyond Mn, the extra electrons enter half-filled d orbitals and are paired, and the higher nuclear charge holds the d electrons more strongly, so the highest state falls: Fe +6, Ni +4, Zn +2.
Why not the others: (B) The lanthanoid contraction affects the elements that follow the lanthanoids (the 5d series), not the 3d series. (C) The 4s electrons are used by all these metals; Zn shows +2 by using exactly its two 4s electrons. (D) Ionisation enthalpies generally rise, not fall, across the series as the nuclear charge increases.
Key point: Highest oxidation state = number of (4s + 3d) electrons up to Mn, then it falls as d electrons pair.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Werner's theory: primary and secondary valences from precipitation and conductivity
questions.question: Compound X has the composition \(\ce{CoCl3.5NH3}\). One mole of X in water gives two moles of AgCl with excess \(\ce{AgNO3}\). Compound Y has the composition \(\ce{PtCl4.2NH3}\). Its solution does not conduct electricity and gives no precipitate with \(\ce{AgNO3}\). According to Werner's theory, which description is correct?
options: A) X is \(\ce{[Co(NH3)5]Cl3}\) and gives four ions per formula unit; platinum in Y has coordination number 6
B) X is \(\ce{[Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2}\) and gives three ions per formula unit; Y is \(\ce{[Pt(NH3)2Cl2]Cl2}\) with coordination number 4
C) X is \(\ce{[Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2}\) and gives three ions per formula unit; Y is \(\ce{[Pt(NH3)2Cl4]}\) with coordination number 6
D) X is \(\ce{[Co(NH3)5Cl2]Cl}\) and gives two ions per formula unit; Y is \(\ce{[Pt(NH3)2Cl4]}\) with coordination number 6
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) X is \(\ce{[Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2}\) and gives three ions per formula unit; Y is \(\ce{[Pt(NH3)2Cl4]}\) with coordination number 6.
Concept: Werner proposed that a metal shows a primary (ionisable) valence and a secondary (non-ionisable) valence. Groups held by secondary valences are written inside the square bracket and are not precipitated. The secondary valence is the coordination number. Only chloride ions outside the bracket are precipitated by \(\ce{AgNO3}\).
Why: X gives 2 mol of AgCl, so two chlorides are outside the bracket and one is inside with the five ammonia molecules: \(\ce{[Co(NH3)5Cl]Cl2}\). In water it gives \(\ce{[Co(NH3)5Cl]^2+}\) and \(\ce{2Cl-}\), three ions. Y gives no AgCl and does not conduct, so no chloride is ionisable and no ions are formed: all four chlorides and both ammonia molecules are bonded to platinum, \(\ce{[Pt(NH3)2Cl4]}\), coordination number \(2+4=6\).
Why not the others: (A) \(\ce{[Co(NH3)5]Cl3}\) would give 3 mol of AgCl, and cobalt would have coordination number 5 instead of 6. (B) \(\ce{[Pt(NH3)2Cl2]Cl2}\) would conduct and give 2 mol of AgCl. (D) \(\ce{[Co(NH3)5Cl2]Cl}\) would give only 1 mol of AgCl, and cobalt would have seven groups attached.
Key point: Moles of AgCl = chlorides outside the bracket; coordination number = groups inside the bracket.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Boiling points of halomethanes and the nature of the C–X bond
questions.question: The boiling points of the halomethanes increase in the order \(\ce{CH3F}<\ce{CH3Cl}<\ce{CH3Br}<\ce{CH3I}\), although the polarity of the C–X bond decreases from fluorine to iodine. What is the reason?
options: A) The C–X bond enthalpy increases from fluorine to iodine, so more heat is needed to boil the liquid
B) van der Waals forces increase with the size and mass of the halogen atom and outweigh the decrease in dipole–dipole attraction
C) Iodomethane forms hydrogen bonds with its neighbours, and fluoromethane does not
D) The solubility in water increases from fluoromethane to iodomethane
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) van der Waals forces increase with the size and mass of the halogen atom and outweigh the decrease in dipole–dipole attraction.
Concept: The boiling point of a molecular liquid depends on the forces between molecules, not on the strength of the bonds inside a molecule. Haloalkanes attract one another by dipole–dipole and van der Waals forces. For the same alkyl group the boiling points follow the order RI > RBr > RCl > RF.
Why: From fluorine to iodine the halogen atom becomes larger and has more electrons, so the molecule is more easily polarised and the van der Waals forces become stronger. This increase is larger than the loss of dipole–dipole attraction caused by the lower polarity of the bond, so the boiling point rises.
Why not the others: (A) The C–X bond enthalpy decreases, not increases, from C–F to C–I, and boiling does not break this bond. (C) Hydrogen bonding needs hydrogen attached to F, O or N; none of these molecules has it. (D) Haloalkanes are only slightly soluble in water, and solubility in water does not decide the boiling point of the pure liquid.
Key point: Boiling point follows intermolecular forces: RI > RBr > RCl > RF.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Hydroboration–oxidation of an alkene: product and mass obtained
questions.question: 8.4 g of propene (molar mass 42 g mol⁻¹) is treated with diborane and then with hydrogen peroxide in aqueous sodium hydroxide. The alcohol (molar mass 60 g mol⁻¹) is obtained in 75% yield. Which alcohol is formed, and what mass is obtained?
options: A) Propan-2-ol; 9.0 g
B) Propan-1-ol; 12.0 g
C) Propan-2-ol; 12.0 g
D) Propan-1-ol; 9.0 g
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Propan-1-ol; 9.0 g.
Concept: In hydroboration–oxidation, diborane adds to the double bond and the product is oxidised to an alcohol by hydrogen peroxide in aqueous sodium hydroxide. The alcohol formed looks as if water has added to the alkene in a way opposite to Markovnikov's rule.
Given: \(m_{propene}=8.4\) g; \(M_{propene}=42\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}\); \(M_{alcohol}=60\ \mathrm{g\,mol^{-1}}\); yield = 75%.
Formula/Principle: \(\ce{CH3-CH=CH2 ->[(i)\ B2H6][(ii)\ H2O2,\ OH-] CH3-CH2-CH2-OH}\); mass = moles × yield × molar mass.
Step 1: \(n_{propene}=\dfrac{8.4}{42}=0.20\) mol.
Step 2: Moles of alcohol obtained \(=0.20\times0.75=0.15\) mol.
Step 3: \[m=0.15\times60=9.0\ \text{g of propan-1-ol}\]
Why: Boron attaches to the carbon atom that has more hydrogen atoms (the end carbon), and the –OH group takes its place, so the primary alcohol is formed.
Why not the others: (A) Propan-2-ol is the product of acid-catalysed hydration (Markovnikov addition), not of hydroboration–oxidation. (B) 12.0 g is the mass for 100% yield. (C) It has both the wrong alcohol and the mass for 100% yield.
Key point: Hydroboration–oxidation gives the anti-Markovnikov alcohol.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Preparation of aldehydes: Rosenmund reduction, Stephen reaction and ozonolysis
questions.question:
Consider three preparations.
(i) Benzoyl chloride + \(\ce{H2}\) over Pd on \(\ce{BaSO4}\)
(ii) Ethanenitrile + \(\ce{SnCl2}\)/HCl, followed by hydrolysis
(iii) But-2-ene + \(\ce{O3}\), followed by Zn/\(\ce{H2O}\)
Which statement is correct?
options: A) (i) gives benzyl alcohol, because hydrogen over palladium reduces an acyl chloride completely
B) (ii) and (iii) give the same aldehyde, ethanal; in (i) barium sulphate lowers the activity of palladium so that reduction stops at benzaldehyde
C) (ii) gives ethanamine and (iii) gives ethanol
D) (iii) gives a mixture of propanone and methanal
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (ii) and (iii) give the same aldehyde, ethanal; in (i) barium sulphate lowers the activity of palladium so that reduction stops at benzaldehyde.
Concept: Rosenmund reduction: an acyl chloride is hydrogenated over palladium on barium sulphate to an aldehyde. Stephen reaction: a nitrile is reduced by stannous chloride and hydrochloric acid to an imine, which gives an aldehyde on hydrolysis. Ozonolysis of an alkene followed by zinc and water gives aldehydes or ketones by breaking the double bond.
Why: (i) \(\ce{C6H5COCl + H2 ->[Pd-BaSO4] C6H5CHO + HCl}\). (ii) \(\ce{CH3CN ->[SnCl2,\ HCl] CH3CH=NH ->[H3O+] CH3CHO}\). (iii) \(\ce{CH3CH=CHCH3 ->[(i)\ O3][(ii)\ Zn,\ H2O] 2CH3CHO}\). So (ii) and (iii) both give ethanal. Barium sulphate partly poisons the palladium, which prevents further reduction of the aldehyde to the alcohol.
Why not the others: (A) With the poisoned catalyst the reduction stops at benzaldehyde; benzyl alcohol would need an unpoisoned catalyst or a stronger reducing agent. (C) Ethanamine would need complete reduction of the nitrile, and ozonolysis with zinc and water gives carbonyl compounds, not alcohols. (D) But-2-ene is symmetrical, with one hydrogen and one methyl group on each doubly bonded carbon, so it gives two molecules of ethanal.
Key point: Rosenmund, Stephen and reductive ozonolysis all stop at the aldehyde stage.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Basic strength of amines in aqueous solution
questions.question: Which is the correct order of basic strength in aqueous solution, with the reason?
options: A) \(\ce{(CH3)2NH}>\ce{CH3NH2}>\ce{(CH3)3N}>\ce{NH3}>\ce{C6H5NH2}\); the +I effect, solvation of the cation and steric hindrance act together, and in aniline the lone pair is delocalised into the ring
B) \(\ce{(CH3)3N}>\ce{(CH3)2NH}>\ce{CH3NH2}>\ce{NH3}>\ce{C6H5NH2}\); basic strength depends only on the number of methyl groups
C) \(\ce{C6H5NH2}>\ce{NH3}>\ce{CH3NH2}>\ce{(CH3)2NH}>\ce{(CH3)3N}\); the phenyl group donates electrons to nitrogen
D) \(\ce{NH3}>\ce{CH3NH2}>\ce{(CH3)2NH}>\ce{(CH3)3N}>\ce{C6H5NH2}\); methyl groups withdraw electrons from nitrogen
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(\ce{(CH3)2NH}>\ce{CH3NH2}>\ce{(CH3)3N}>\ce{NH3}>\ce{C6H5NH2}\); the +I effect, solvation of the cation and steric hindrance act together, and in aniline the lone pair is delocalised into the ring.
Concept: An amine is a base because of the lone pair on nitrogen. Alkyl groups push electrons towards nitrogen (+I effect) and make the amine more basic than ammonia. In water the ammonium ion formed is stabilised by hydrogen bonding with water; the more N–H bonds it has, the better it is solvated. Bulky groups hinder solvation.
Why: By the +I effect alone the order would be tertiary > secondary > primary. By solvation alone it would be primary > secondary > tertiary. The two effects together, with steric hindrance, give \(\ce{(CH3)2NH}>\ce{CH3NH2}>\ce{(CH3)3N}\) for the methyl amines, all stronger than ammonia. In aniline the lone pair on nitrogen is in resonance with the benzene ring and is less available, so aniline is the weakest.
Why not the others: (B) This is the order in the gas phase, where there is no solvation; in water the tertiary amine falls below the primary amine. (C) The phenyl group withdraws the lone pair by resonance; it does not make nitrogen richer in electrons. (D) Methyl groups release electrons; they make the amines stronger bases than ammonia, not weaker.
Key point: In water: (CH3)2NH > CH3NH2 > (CH3)3N > NH3 > C6H5NH2.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Evidence for the cyclic structure of glucose
questions.question:
Four observations on glucose are listed.
(i) With HI on prolonged heating it gives n-hexane.
(ii) Bromine water oxidises it to gluconic acid.
(iii) With acetic anhydride it gives a pentaacetate.
(iv) The pentaacetate does not react with hydroxylamine.
Which observation cannot be explained by the open-chain structure \(\ce{HOCH2(CHOH)4CHO}\), and what explains it?
options: A) (i); a six-membered ring is needed to give a six-carbon straight chain
B) (ii); gluconic acid shows that glucose has a ketone group
C) (iv); there is no free –CHO group, because C-1 is part of a cyclic hemiacetal formed with the –OH group on C-5
D) (iii); a pentaacetate shows that glucose has six –OH groups
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (iv); there is no free –CHO group, because C-1 is part of a cyclic hemiacetal formed with the –OH group on C-5.
Concept: The open-chain structure of glucose has a straight chain of six carbon atoms, five –OH groups and one –CHO group. It explains most reactions of glucose but not all. Glucose exists mainly as a six-membered cyclic hemiacetal in which the –OH on C-5 has added to the –CHO group.
Why: (i) n-Hexane shows six carbon atoms in a straight chain. (ii) Mild oxidation to a six-carbon acid shows a –CHO group. (iii) A pentaacetate shows five –OH groups. All three fit the open chain. But the open-chain pentaacetate would still have a free –CHO group and should react with hydroxylamine to give an oxime. It does not, so the –CHO group is not free: C-1 is held in a ring as a hemiacetal, and in the pentaacetate the ring cannot open.
Why not the others: (A) A straight chain of six carbons is exactly what the open-chain structure predicts. (B) Bromine water oxidises an aldehyde group, not a ketone group, to a carboxylic acid with the same number of carbon atoms. (D) Five acetate groups show five –OH groups, which the open-chain structure has.
Key point: No reaction of glucose pentaacetate with NH2OH → no free –CHO → cyclic hemiacetal structure.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Domain and range of a relation defined on a finite set
questions.question: Let \(A=\{1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8\}\). For a positive integer \(k\), let \(R_k=\{(x,y)\in A\times A: xy=k\}\). For which values of \(k\) does the domain of \(R_k\) have exactly three elements?
options: A) \(k=4\) and \(k=16\) only
C) \(k=16\) only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \(k=4\) and \(k=16\) only.
Given: \(A=\{1,\dots,8\},\quad R_k=\{(x,y)\in A\times A:\ xy=k\}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\operatorname{dom}R_k=\{d:\ d\mid k,\ 1\le d\le8,\ 1\le\tfrac kd\le8\};\quad(d,\tfrac kd)\in R_k\iff(\tfrac kd,d)\in R_k\)
Step 1: \(\text{elements of the domain pair up as}\ d\leftrightarrow\tfrac kd;\ \text{an odd count needs}\ d=\tfrac kd\Rightarrow k=d^2\)
Step 2: \(k\in\{1,4,9,16,25,36,49,64\}\)
Step 3: \(k=4:\ \{1,2,4\}\ (3);\quad k=16:\ \{2,4,8\}\ (3)\)
Step 4: \(k=1:\ \{1\};\ k=9:\ \{3\}\ (\tfrac91=9>8);\ k=25:\ \{5\};\ k=36:\ \{6\}\ (\tfrac{36}4=9>8);\ k=49:\ \{7\};\ k=64:\ \{8\}\)
Worked derivation: \[|\operatorname{dom}R_k|=3\iff k\in\{4,16\}\]
Check: \[R_4=\{(1,4),(2,2),(4,1)\},\qquad R_{16}=\{(2,8),(4,4),(8,2)\}\]
Why: \(xy=k\ \text{is symmetric in}\ x\ \text{and}\ y,\ \text{so the domain equals the range}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(k=9:\ (1,9)\notin A\times A\Rightarrow\operatorname{dom}=\{3\}\); (C) \(k=4\ \text{also gives}\ \{1,2,4\}\); (D) \(k=36:\ (4,9),(9,4)\notin A\times A\Rightarrow\operatorname{dom}=\{6\}\).
Key point: \(\text{both}\ d\ \text{and}\ \tfrac kd\ \text{must lie in}\ A\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Domain and range of a real function with a square root
questions.question: Let \(f(x)=\sqrt{9-x^2}\) be a real function. How many integers are there in its domain and in its range, respectively?
options: A) 7 and 7
B) 6 and 3
C) 7 and 4
D) 9 and 4
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 7 and 4.
Given: \(f(x)=\sqrt{9-x^2}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\sqrt u\ \text{is real}\iff u\ge0\)
Step 1: \(9-x^2\ge0\Rightarrow-3\le x\le3\Rightarrow\text{domain}=[-3,3]\)
Step 2: \(\text{integers in the domain}:\ -3,-2,-1,0,1,2,3\ (7)\)
Step 3: \(0\le9-x^2\le9\Rightarrow0\le f(x)\le3\Rightarrow\text{range}=[0,3]\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{integers in the range}:\ 0,1,2,3\ (4)\]
Check: \[f(\pm3)=0,\quad f(0)=3,\quad f(\pm\sqrt5)=2,\quad f(\pm2\sqrt2)=1\]
Why: \(\text{the graph is the upper half of the circle}\ x^2+y^2=9\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{range}\ne[-3,3]:\ \sqrt{\ }\ge0\); (B) \(\text{end points}\ \pm3\ \text{and}\ 0,3\ \text{are included}\); (D) \(|x|\le3,\ \text{not}\ |x|\le4\).
Key point: \(y=\sqrt{a^2-x^2}:\ \text{domain}\ [-a,a],\ \text{range}\ [0,a]\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Counting solutions with the graph of the sine function
questions.question: How many real solutions does the equation \(\sin x=\dfrac{x}{20}\) have?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 11.
Given: \(\sin x=\dfrac x{20}\)
Formula/Principle: \(|\sin x|\le1\Rightarrow|x|\le20;\quad\text{both sides are odd functions}\)
Step 1: \(x=0\ \text{is a solution};\ \text{count}\ x>0\ \text{and double}\)
Step 2: \(\sin x>0\ \text{on}\ (0,\pi),\ (2\pi,3\pi),\ (4\pi,5\pi),\ (6\pi,7\pi);\quad6\pi\approx18.85,\ 7\pi\approx21.99\)
Step 3: \((0,\pi):\ \text{slope of}\ \tfrac x{20}\ \text{at}\ 0\ \text{is}\ \tfrac1{20}<1,\ \text{and}\ \tfrac\pi{20}>\sin\pi=0\Rightarrow1\ \text{solution}\)
Step 4: \((2\pi,3\pi):\ \tfrac{2.5\pi}{20}\approx0.39<1\Rightarrow2;\qquad(4\pi,5\pi):\ \tfrac{4.5\pi}{20}\approx0.71<1\Rightarrow2\)
